title: Don't Allow Team Members to Delegate Up
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece warns leaders against a specific pattern of exploitation: team members who effectively 'delegate up' their own problems to an accommodating, conflict-avoidant leader, who then ends up doing everyone else's work in addition to their own. The author distinguishes this from healthy support, arguing that offering advice and removing obstacles is legitimate leadership, but that owning and solving other people's problems for them crosses a line into unhealthy dependence. The piece frames boundary-setting as the leader's own responsibility, since no one can be exploited without allowing it.
points: Kind, accommodating, or conflict-avoidant leaders are especially vulnerable to team members who effectively 'delegate up' their own problems.
There's a clear line between offering advice or removing obstacles (legitimate leadership) and actually owning or solving someone else's task for them.
No one can be taken advantage of unless they allow it — leaders retain the power to set boundaries and refuse to play along at any point.
Good leaders delegate down and refuse to let team members delegate up, staying helpful without doing others' work for them.
quotes: Leaders who are kind, generous, conflict-avoidant, tolerant, and too busy can be exploited by those who want to get their way.
It is wise to remember that no one can be taken advantage of unless they let the other party do so.
Leaders who allow team members and colleagues to delegate their problems up soon find themselves doing everyone else’s work in addition to their own.
Offering assistance is not the same thing as solving or working on an issue others should be accountable for.
Good leaders delegate down and refuse to let team members delegate up. They are helpful and supportive, but never do other people’s work.
